# 10. Position: the model reads a set Everything so far has answered the first of the two questions the model asks about an incoming token: **what the token is**. The second question is **where it is**, and the reason it needs a separate answer is *structural rather than incidental*. Attention, as Session 2 built it, computes a score between every pair of positions from their query and key vectors and mixes values according to those scores. **Nothing in that computation refers to the order of the sequence.** Permute the input tokens and every pairwise score permutes with them, and the output permutes correspondingly: the mechanism is **equivariant to permutation**, which is a precise way of saying it cannot tell *"dog bites man"* from *"man bites dog"*. > **The transformer does not read a sequence. It reads a set**, and order has to be supplied to it deliberately. Session 2's minor topic already *demonstrated* this rather than asserting it, by training two tiny models side by side on a task rigged so every sequence appeared once with each label under a swap of two tokens. The **token-only** model was pinned at chance, because the two cases were *literally identical inputs* to it. The **token-plus-position** model learned the rule. That experiment is the foundation this section builds on, and the question now is **what the position signal should be made of**.
# 11. The absolute table, and the wall at max_position The simplest answer is the one that mirrors what we just built for tokens: keep a second table, indexed by position instead of by identifier, and add its row to the token's row before the stack sees either. ```python token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model) position_embedding = nn.Embedding(max_position, d_model) x = token_embedding(token_ids) + position_embedding(torch.arange(T)) ``` This is what **GPT-2** did and it works. It is also, as a parameter block, small enough to ignore next to the vocabulary table, since `max_position` is thousands rather than hundreds of thousands. **So the objection to it is not cost.** The objection is that it inherits the property from Section 2 that we spent that section learning to be careful about. **A position table is gathered and scatter-added exactly like a token table**, so row `t` learns only from steps in which some sequence had a token at position `t`. If the model is trained with a maximum position of **4,096**, then rows 0 through 4,095 are trained and **row 7,000 does not exist**. Extend the context at inference and there is no row to fetch; allocate the rows in advance and never train them, and they sit at their **random initialisation and inject noise at exactly the positions you extended the model to handle**. > **The table cannot extrapolate, and the reason is not subtle or fixable by better training.** There is no signal in the parameters that connects row 4,095 to row 4,096, because they were only ever *independent rows in a lookup table*. That is a **hard wall**, and it is the wall the entire modern positional-encoding literature exists to get past. The way past it is to **stop storing position and start computing it**, so that position enters through a *function of `t`* defined for every `t` rather than through a row that exists only for the values seen in training. The original Transformer's **sinusoidal** encoding was the first version of that idea. What the field converged on afterwards, and what V5 will actually use, is the subject of the next class.
> An **absolute position table trained live in the browser** on a task whose answer depends on where a token sits. Training runs on positions zero through seven with real gradients, and the model learns the rule to near-perfect accuracy inside that range. A second panel evaluates the same trained model at positions eight through fifteen, where accuracy falls to chance, and a coverage strip shows why: those rows never appeared in a batch, so the scatter-add never wrote to them and they hold their initialisation. The cliff at the trained boundary is measured, not drawn.
# 12. The families, and what Session 8 builds It is worth ending the positional thread with a map rather than a mechanism, because the mechanisms are next week's material and the map is what makes them arrive as answers rather than as a list. There are broadly **four places a position signal can be injected**: 1. **Stored and added at the input.** The absolute learned table we just built and just watched fail. 2. **Computed and added at the input.** The sinusoidal scheme, which extrapolates in the weak sense that the function is defined everywhere, though a model trained only on short sequences has still never had to *use* the far part of the function. 3. **Applied inside attention to the queries and keys**, so the score between two positions depends on their **offset** rather than their absolute indices. This is where the **rotary** family lives and where the field has settled. 4. **Applied to the attention scores directly** as a distance-dependent bias, which is the **ALiBi** family. The trade running across all four is between **how much the model is told and how much it has to infer**. A signal that is **stored** is maximally expressive within its trained range and *useless outside it*. A signal that is **computed** generalises by construction but *constrains what can be represented*. > That is the **same trade this session made twice already**, once when a dense table became a factorized one and once when a factorized table became a Kronecker one. It is not a coincidence: it is what happens **every time structure is substituted for stored parameters**. Session 8 takes this apart properly. It builds rotary position embeddings and the scaling schemes that extend them, it covers the attention-side variants that change which pairs get computed at all, and it treats long-context extension as its own engineering problem rather than as a larger number in a config. Today's job was to hand it a model whose input representation is decided and whose positional wall is felt rather than described.

Selecting a family traces the signal through the model to the point where attention consumes it. # 13. The V5 embedding decision The session commits to a design, and the design is the following. - **Vocabulary** stays in the **131K class** inherited from the BrahmicTokenizer work, chosen against fertility across the target scripts *and* against the parameter arithmetic in Section 3 together, not against either alone. - **Input path** is the released **Kronecker byte codec plus a trainable projection**, with a dense table as the **control arm**. The `pos_dim` window is chosen by *measurement rather than by default*, starting from the shipped value of 32. - **The projection is trainable throughout.** The codec is already frozen by construction, so freezing the projection as well leaves the input path with *no adaptive capacity at all*. Freezing is a scheduled and logged decision, never a residue of an experiment. - **Output head is untied**, because at V5's scale the saving from tying is small and the constraint on the geometry is not, and because a structured input path and a dense output head are not naturally the same object anyway. - **The byte window is an architectural parameter**, not a default to inherit. Section 8 showed that 32 bytes is 32 English characters but only 10 Indic ones, so `pos_dim` is set by a collision count measured on the real V5 vocabulary, per script. - **Position policy** is deferred to Session 8 by design, with the absolute table **ruled out** for the long-context target on the evidence in Section 11. All of it is written into the ledger under `embedding_policy_id`, so any checkpoint can answer what its input path was doing when it was written. > **Every number above is a hypothesis.** Session 5 established the standard the cohort holds itself to on data decisions, which is that *a proportion is an opinion until a proxy run has tested it*, and there is **no reason an architecture decision should be held to a lower standard than a mixture decision**. The byte window, the projection width and the tying decision all get proxy runs at the **one-billion and three-billion scale** before any of them is trusted at full scale.
> A **V5 embedding design board** that assembles the full policy and computes its consequences from real arithmetic rather than from a score table. Choosing a vocabulary, width, input path, rank, tying and freeze policy produces the parameter count, the training memory with full optimizer accounting, the compression against dense, and the degrees of freedom per token that the chosen structure leaves.
